definition: The layered arrangement of computer storage, such as registers, CPU caches, DRAM and persistent storage. Smaller, lower-latency levels are backed by larger ones; locality can make many requests hit near the processor.
example: A conventional serial lookup model checks L1, then lower caches; a miss can obtain data from DRAM or another coherent cache.

definition: A hardware-managed memory that retains copies of instruction or data lines to reduce the need for lower-level accesses. Cache residency, policy and access pattern determine whether an access benefits; processors can also have specialised caches for decoded instructions or branch targets.
example: A design may have private L1 caches and a last-level cache shared among cores; the exact organisation is processor-specific.

definition: The tendency to reuse the same addresses soon (temporal locality) or nearby addresses close together in time (spatial locality). It helps a smaller cache serve a useful share of accesses.
example: A loop summing an array has spatial locality; its running total has temporal locality.

definition: Locality in time: data used recently is likely to be used again soon. Caches exploit it by keeping recently used data and evicting data that has not been used for a while.
example: A repeatedly used loop counter illustrates temporal reuse; an optimiser may keep it in a register, while memory residency depends on the cache policy and other accesses.

definition: Locality in space: after using one address, a program is likely to use nearby addresses soon. Caches exploit it by fetching a whole cache line (often 64 bytes) rather than single bytes.
example: With an aligned array of eight-byte doubles and a 64-byte line, fetching element zero supplies the line containing elements zero through seven.

definition: Solid-state drive: persistent storage commonly built from NAND flash, accessed through an I/O interface. Its latency, throughput and durability depend on the device and workload; it is a different layer from ordinary volatile DRAM.
An access whose data is already present in the cache level being checked, so it is served there without going further down the hierarchy.
The fraction of accesses to a cache level that hit: hits divided by accesses. It is often written as a percentage, and it is always one minus the miss rate.
example: 950 hits out of 1,000 accesses is a hit rate of 95 %.

definition: The fraction of accesses to a cache level that miss: misses divided by accesses, equal to one minus the hit rate. A level's local miss rate counts only the accesses that reached that level; its global miss rate counts them against every access the processor made.
example: In an aligned cold demand-only scan, four-byte ints with 64-byte lines miss once per sixteen scalar accesses, or 6.25%, with no interference or prefetching.

definition: The extra time a cache miss costs compared with a hit: the time to get the line from the next level down. It is measured in clock cycles or nanoseconds.
example: If L1 hits take 4 cycles and fetching from L2 adds 10 more, the L1 miss penalty is 10 cycles.

definition: The data and code referenced during a chosen interval of execution. Fitting within a cache’s capacity makes reuse possible, but set conflicts, interference, coherence and replacement can still cause misses.
example: A repeatedly scanned 16 KiB table fits within a 32 KiB data capacity; that capacity check alone does not guarantee hits.

definition: A sharp change in performance near a resource limit, such as an increasing working set exhausting useful cache residency. The location and shape depend on the workload, mapping, prefetching and other interference; cache-capacity steps are not guaranteed.
The standard, reference implementation of the Python language, written in C. Its lists store references (pointers) to separately allocated objects rather than the values themselves.

A compiler optimisation that replaces a function call with the function's body. It can remove call overhead and enable further simplification; duplicated code can also increase instruction-cache pressure, though the final code need not always grow.
An electronic component that stores electric charge. Conventional DRAM uses charge in a cell capacitor to encode a bit; which charge state represents zero or one depends on the cell design.

The distance in bytes or elements between consecutive accesses. Unit stride over a dense array uses neighbouring elements; a stride at least one cache line apart uses different lines on successive accesses, while residency determines whether they hit.
example: Walking down a column of a 1024 × 1024 array of doubles has a stride of 8,192 bytes.

definition: A loop transformation that divides work into smaller blocks so data can be reused before eviction. The useful bytes fitting in cache is necessary for the simple model but does not rule out line fragmentation, set conflicts or interference.
example: Three square tiles of 32 by 32 eight-byte doubles contain 24 KiB of useful data; their strided line footprint and set mapping still need checking.

definition: Exchanging the nesting order of loops to change locality or expose other optimisation opportunities. It is valid only when dependencies and the required numerical semantics permit the change.
example: Changing ijk to ikj cuts model misses in matrix multiply from 1.125 to 0.25 per iteration.

definition: Combining compatible loops over related data so reuse occurs sooner and loop overhead may fall. Dependencies, side effects and numerical requirements must permit the transformation.

Array of structures: a data layout where each record's fields are stored together, one record after another. Good when code uses most fields of a record at once; wasteful when a pass touches only one or two fields.
example: A 32-byte Particle struct in an array: a pass that reads only x and vx uses 8 of every 32 bytes fetched.

definition: Structure of arrays: a layout with a separate dense array for each field. Scanning one field can avoid fetching unused record fields and can support SIMD vectorisation; alignment, the operation and compiler determine the result.
example: Separate x[] and vx[] arrays mean a pass doing x += vx × dt uses every byte it fetches.

definition: Reorganising a data structure so the frequently used (hot) fields sit together in a compact struct and the rarely used (cold) fields are moved elsewhere, such as behind a pointer. More useful records then fit in each cache line.

The IEEE 754 binary64 format uses 64 bits, or eight bytes, with 53 bits of significand precision. Many C implementations use it for double and NumPy names it float64; the C language alone does not require every double to be binary64.
example: A 64-byte cache line holds 8 doubles.

definition: The IEEE 754 binary32 format uses 32 bits, or four bytes, with 24 bits of significand precision. Many C implementations use it for float; the C language alone does not require that representation.
A long-established programming language for numerical and scientific computing. Its arrays are column-major, and its indices start at 1 by default.
A commercial numerical computing environment and language. Like Fortran, it stores matrices in column-major order.
A programming language used for numerical and scientific computing. Its ordinary dense multidimensional Array type uses column-major storage; custom array types and views may have other layouts.

Fast Fourier transform: an algorithm family for computing discrete Fourier transforms efficiently. Power-of-two transforms are common but not required by every FFT algorithm or library; their access patterns can interact with cache mapping.

An open column-oriented file format for efficient analytical storage and processing. Grouping values by column can avoid reading unrelated columns, although metadata, encoding and I/O granularity also affect bytes read.
Storing table values grouped by column rather than by whole row. Selecting a few columns can reduce unrelated data reads, though encoding, metadata and I/O granularity affect the actual traffic.

Combining matrices so each output element sums products from one input row and one input column. The conventional triple-loop algorithm for square matrices performs a cubic number of multiply-add updates; faster asymptotic algorithms also exist.

Bringing a cache line into a cache from another part of the memory hierarchy, such as a lower cache, DRAM or a coherent peer. Counting fills can model incoming traffic when the transfer assumptions are explicit.
example: A cold aligned demand-only scan of 4,000,000 bytes with 64-byte lines needs 62,500 line fills, assuming no extra traffic.

definition: A cache initially lacking the data under discussion. First line allocations miss in a demand-only model; warming does not guarantee that a large or conflicting working set remains resident.

Representing a primitive value with an object, such as Java Integer. Collections of boxed values hold references that can point to distinct or shared objects, adding indirection; object layout depends on the runtime.
Java's resizable list class. It stores references to objects, so an ArrayList of Integer holds pointers to boxed Integer objects rather than raw ints.

A C++ sequence container whose elements, except the specialised vector<bool> representation, are stored contiguously. Contiguous traversal can improve locality; reallocation and element type affect its behaviour.
A cache coherence protocol giving each cache line one of four states: Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid. Its Exclusive state lets a core write data nobody else holds without sending a request.
example: A line read by one core alone arrives in E; a later write changes it silently to M.

definition: The simplest common coherence protocol, with three states: Modified, Shared and Invalid. Without an Exclusive state, reading then writing private data costs two requests.

An extension of MESI with a fifth state, Owned: dirty data that other caches may also share. The owner supplies the data to readers and remains responsible for writing it back, deferring a write to memory.

A cache coherence protocol family extending MESI with a Forward state for a designated clean responder. A Forward copy can supply later sharing requests; exact routing and what happens when no Forward copy remains are implementation-specific.

In textbook MESI, a valid line with exclusive write permission whose data is dirty relative to its backing level. Other caches must acquire the current data through the coherence protocol before using it.
In textbook MESI, a sole clean cached copy relative to the relevant backing level. A local write can change it to Modified without a separate ownership-upgrade request.
The MESI state meaning the line is clean and other caches may also hold copies. Reads hit locally, but a write must first invalidate the other copies.
The MESI state meaning the cache entry holds no usable data for that line, so any access to it misses.

The extra MOESI state: dirty data with possible Shared copies in other caches. The owner can supply readers and retains responsibility for preserving or handing over the current data; a backing-level update can be deferred.

A clean cached copy designated to forward data in a MESIF protocol. It can serve a later sharing request without requiring all clean sharers to respond; an implementation can obtain data elsewhere if no suitable Forward copy remains.

Bus read: in the textbook MESI bus model used here, a request to read a line absent from the requesting cache. A Modified peer supplies current data and moves to Shared; the model also updates the backing level so its shared copies are clean.

Bus read exclusive: the textbook coherence request a cache sends when it wants to write a line it does not hold. It fetches the line and makes every other cache invalidate its copy (a read for ownership).
Bus upgrade: the textbook coherence request a cache sends when it already holds a line in Shared and wants to write it. Other caches invalidate their copies; no data needs transferring.
A coherence approach in which a core must invalidate all other copies of a line before writing it, so it becomes the only holder. MESI and its variants are write-invalidate protocols.
A coherence approach in which a write sends the new data to every cache holding a copy, instead of invalidating them. It can cost more traffic when one core writes repeatedly.

The rules for permitted observations and ordering of memory operations, including operations on different locations. Hardware models such as x86-TSO differ from language-level atomic and data-race rules; coherence alone supplies only a per-location order.

An architectural model for ordinary x86 write-back memory: stores are observed in order, while a later load from a different location may complete before an older buffered store is visible elsewhere. Special memory types and non-temporal operations require their documented ordering rules.

A coherence approach in which participating caches observe an ordered stream of coherence requests and check whether they hold the requested line. A textbook shared-bus implementation broadcasts requests; modern fabrics can use filtering and other routing.

A coherence mechanism that records actual or possible holders of a line and directs requests to the relevant candidates. Its tracking and routing can reduce broadcast traffic, at the cost of metadata and extra protocol steps.
A hardware structure that tracks possible holders of cache lines to avoid unnecessary coherence probes. Its coverage, precision and benefit depend on the implementation.
A cache miss caused because another core's write invalidated a line this cache previously held. It is a fourth kind of miss, beyond compulsory, capacity and conflict misses.

Concurrent accesses to the same logical data, with at least one writer, that require communication or synchronisation. Separating unrelated variables cannot remove this communication; private accumulation or batching can reduce its frequency.
Repeated ownership changes of a coherence line between cores that write it. One core can perform many writes while it retains ownership; the term does not imply a transfer on every individual store.

Arm’s AMBA Coherent Hub Interface: a protocol for coherent interconnects used in multicore systems. Its message and permission scheme supports coherent communication among participating components; its details differ from the textbook MESI bus model.
The wiring and protocol that connects cores, caches and memory controllers on a chip (and between chips), carrying coherence requests and data.

A C/C++ atomic operation using memory_order_relaxed: it remains indivisible and participates in that atomic object’s modification-order/coherence rules, but does not by itself synchronise other memory. A relaxed polling load can check a lock value; successfully taking the lock still needs the appropriate acquire operation.

C/C++ atomic orderings used for synchronisation. A release operation can synchronise with a matching acquire that reads from its release sequence, creating a happens-before relationship for surrounding ordinary accesses; these operations are not universal fences for every thread.
A lock that waiting threads acquire by looping (spinning) until it becomes free, rather than sleeping. Under contention a naive one generates heavy coherence traffic.

A spinlock strategy that first polls with atomic reads, attempts an acquire read-modify-write when the lock looks free, and releases with release ordering. Read polling can reduce ownership traffic while the line stays shared; it does not eliminate contention.
A queue-based spinlock (named after Mellor-Crummey and Scott) in which each waiter spins on its own node, so a release disturbs only the next waiter instead of every contender.

A region that accesses shared state under the synchronisation rules needed to protect it. A mutual-exclusion lock admits only one holder at a time; other designs, such as reader/writer protection, allow compatible readers.
A counter or partial result updated by one thread, then combined under suitable synchronisation. It reduces shared writes; storage for separate threads must also avoid harmful false sharing.

A counter split into several cells that different threads update, with the total found by adding the cells. It spreads writes over several cache lines to reduce contention; Java's LongAdder works this way.
A Java class that keeps a running sum in several striped cells to reduce contention among updating threads. Its sum() adds the cells and is not an atomic snapshot while updates continue.
A Java class providing atomic operations on one long value. Multiple cores repeatedly updating the same instance can contend for ownership of its cache line; the severity is workload-dependent.

A Rust crossbeam-utils wrapper that pads and aligns a value using a target-dependent estimate intended to reduce false sharing. The fetched documentation uses 128-byte alignment on x86-64, a conservative adjacent-line-prefetch heuristic rather than a measurement of every processor.

A C++17 constant giving an implementation-chosen minimum distance to keep independently written objects apart to avoid false sharing. It is a compile-time hint, not a measurement of the machine running the program.

A Java annotation (sun.misc.Contended in Java 8, jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended from Java 9) that asks the HotSpot JVM to pad a field or class onto its own cache line(s) to avoid false sharing. By default the JVM honours it only inside the JDK; application classes need the JVM flag -XX:-RestrictContended (and, from Java 9, access to the internal package).
Hit Modified: an Intel performance event for a load that finds its line Modified in another core's cache. Many HITM events on one line are a sign of false or true sharing; perf c2c reports them.

An implementation-specific prefetch behaviour that may fetch a neighbouring line, such as an aligned pair of 64-byte lines. It can create additional interaction between separately written neighbouring lines; it does not change the coherence-line size itself.

A physical processor package position in a system. A multi-socket machine can have package-local memory controllers and inter-socket links; one socket can expose several NUMA nodes, so socket and node are different concepts.
POSIX threads: the standard C threading API on Unix-like systems, providing thread creation, joining and locks.

The circuit that translates memory requests requiring DRAM service into device commands and schedules them across memory channels. Cache hits can be served without a DRAM request; controller placement depends on the system.
A group of cache slots (ways) that a given memory line is allowed to occupy. The index bits of an address choose the set; the line can then sit in any way of that set.
example: A 32 KiB, 8-way cache with 64-byte lines has 64 cache sets of 8 ways each.

definition: One slot within a cache set that can hold a single line. The number of ways per set is the cache's associativity.
example: In an 8-way cache each set has 8 ways, so 8 lines that map to the same set can be cached at once.

definition: The number of candidate slots, or ways, for a memory line in a cache. Additional ways can reduce set-placement conflicts but have implementation-dependent latency, power and replacement-policy costs.
example: A direct-mapped cache has associativity 1; a 12-way cache lets each line choose among 12 slots.

definition: A cache in which every memory line has exactly one possible slot, chosen by its index bits. It is simple and fast but two busy lines with the same index keep evicting each other.
example: In a 1 KiB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte lines, addresses 1 KiB apart always fight over the same slot.

definition: A cache divided into sets, where a memory line maps to one set but may occupy any of that set's several ways. It is the usual compromise between direct-mapped and fully associative designs.
example: A 2-way set-associative cache lets two lines with the same index coexist instead of evicting each other.

definition: A cache with a single set, so every line can occupy any slot. There are no set-placement restrictions; lookup implementation and replacement policy still affect cost and miss behaviour.
example: A fully associative LRU cache of the same capacity is the reference used to separate capacity misses from conflict misses.

definition: The high-order address bits stored alongside each cached line. Because many memory lines share one set, the cache compares the requested address's tag with the stored tags to tell which line is actually present.
example: For a 48-bit address with 6 offset and 6 index bits, each line stores a 36-bit tag.

definition: The address bits just above the offset that select which cache set to look in. With S sets it is log base 2 of S bits wide, for example 6 bits for 64 sets.
example: With 64-byte lines and 64 sets, address bits 6 to 11 form the set index.

definition: The lowest address bits, which select a byte within a cache line. A line of L bytes needs log base 2 of L offset bits, for example 6 bits for a 64-byte line.
example: In address 0x678 with 64-byte lines, the low 6 bits 111000 give offset 56.

definition: A status bit indicating whether a cache entry contains usable line data. In the simple tag-lookup model, a matching tag is a hit only when its valid bit is set.
example: An initially empty model cache has every valid bit clear.

definition: A status bit recording that a cached line has data newer than its backing level. Before discarding the last responsible copy, the protocol must preserve the data through a write-back or handover; buffers can overlap that work with other activity.
example: A dirty victim can enter a write-back buffer while the vacated cache slot is reused; this does not discard the modified bytes.

definition: A first-touch miss for a line under the chosen trace and allocation model. Increasing cache capacity or associativity cannot remove that first allocation; prefetching may make the first demand access a hit by moving the transfer earlier.
example: A cold, aligned 64 KiB scan with 64-byte lines has 1,024 first line fills in a demand-only model.

definition: In the conventional three-C classification, a miss on a previously referenced line that also misses in a fully associative LRU reference cache of equal capacity and line size. Blocking and a larger capacity can improve the trace’s reuse.
example: In a demand-only fully associative LRU model, repeatedly scanning all lines of a 64 KiB array through 32 KiB of cache causes misses on every later scan.

definition: In the conventional three-C classification, a previously referenced line misses in the tested cache but hits in a fully associative LRU reference cache of the same capacity and line size. Address mapping and set competition distinguish it from a capacity miss.
example: With simple modulo indexing, two alternating lines 32 KiB apart compete for one slot in a 32 KiB direct-mapped cache.

definition: The conventional classification of cache misses into compulsory, capacity and conflict misses. A first access identifies compulsory misses; comparing later misses with an equal-capacity, equal-line-size fully associative LRU reference distinguishes capacity from conflict misses.
example: A previously seen line that misses here but hits in the specified fully associative LRU reference has a conflict miss.

definition: The rule a cache uses to pick which line in a full set to evict (the victim) when a new line must be brought in. Common choices are LRU, pseudo-LRU, RRIP-style and random.
example: With 8 ways and LRU, the line untouched for longest in that set is evicted.

definition: The line a cache chooses to evict to make room for a newly fetched line. Which line becomes the victim is decided by the replacement policy.
example: In a direct-mapped cache there is no choice: the single occupant of the slot is the victim.

definition: A cheap approximation of least-recently-used replacement. Tree-PLRU keeps a binary tree of bits per set (ways minus one bits, so 7 for 8 ways) that point away from recently used ways; it can pick a different victim from true LRU.
example: An 8-way set with tree-PLRU needs 7 bits, whereas recording the exact LRU order of 8 ways needs at least 16 bits (there are 40,320 possible orders).

definition: Re-reference interval prediction: replacement policies that store a small prediction of how soon each line will be reused. SRRIP and BRRIP choose different insertion predictions; scan resistance is workload-dependent, rather than a promise that no useful line is ever displaced.
example: The original study evaluates two-bit predictions per cache block for its stated workloads and configurations.

definition: A replacement policy that selects a victim using a random or pseudo-random mechanism instead of keeping an exact recency order. It can still perform poorly on particular traces; pseudo-random state and miss handling have costs.
example: A random victim choice needs no LRU-order update on each hit, but can evict a recently useful line.

definition: Virtually indexed, physically tagged cache: virtual bits select candidates while physical tags distinguish memory lines. Keeping simple index and line-offset bits within the page offset avoids synonym-induced different-set copies in that model; other correctness concerns still need handling.
example: With 64-byte lines and 64 sets, all twelve index-plus-offset bits fit inside a 4 KiB page offset. Virtual aliases therefore select the same set in this simple model.

definition: The low address bits that select a byte within a memory page. Address translation never changes them, so they are the same in the virtual and physical address.
example: A 4 KiB page has a 12-bit page offset, because 4,096 is 2 to the power 12.

definition: A circuit that checks a stored cache tag against the requested tag. A conventional parallel set-associative lookup compares every candidate way at once; other lookup organisations can trade comparisons, time and energy.
example: The parallel 8-way lookup model compares eight candidate tags.

definition: The power you must raise 2 to in order to get a given number, written log_2: how many 2s multiplied together make it. It tells you how many bits are needed to number a power-of-two count of things.
example: log_2(64) = 6, so 6 bits number 64 bytes in a line.

definition: The remainder after whole-number division, written mod. Simple caches choose a set as the line number mod the number of sets, which for a power-of-two set count is just the low bits of the line number.

A cache that updates only its own copy on a store, marks the line dirty, and writes it to the next level later, for example when it is evicted or another core requests it. This saves traffic when a line is written many times.
example: In a model with retained ownership and one final eviction, repeated updates of one resident line need one final write-back, not one downstream data write per update.

definition: Adding unused space to change row or array addresses, potentially distributing accesses across cache sets. It uses more storage and can reduce conflict misses when the new mapping suits the access pattern.
example: In the simple 64-set, 64-byte-line example, increasing an 8,192-byte row stride by 64 bytes distributes successive rows across sets.

definition: Average memory access time: the expected time one memory access takes, counting fast cache hits and slower misses together. In the simple blocking model it is the hit time plus the miss rate times the miss penalty.
example: A 4-cycle L1 that misses 5% of the time with a 100-cycle miss penalty has an AMAT of 4 + 0.05 × 100 = 9 cycles.

definition: The time a cache takes to look up an address and return the data when it is present. In the AMAT model it is paid on every access to that level, hit or miss, because the cache is always checked first.
example: An illustrative L1 model can assume a four-cycle lookup; the actual time requires a specified processor and access path.

definition: A cache level's misses divided by the accesses that actually reach that level. For L2 these are only the L1 misses, so the number can look high even when few accesses go to main memory.
example: If 50,000 accesses reach L2 and 10,000 miss, L2's local miss rate is 20%.

definition: A cache level’s misses divided by total requests in the chosen reference stream. For demand-only serial filtering, its global miss rate is the product of local miss rates through and including that level; prefetch, coherence and write-back requests need separate accounting.
example: For demand-only filtering, an L1 local miss rate of 5% and L2 local miss rate of 20% give an L2 global miss rate of 1%.

definition: A cache write policy in which every store updates the cached copy and is also sent on to the next level, possibly via a write buffer. Lines never hold data that the next level lacks once pending writes drain, so no dirty bit is needed.
example: In a no-merging model, three stores send three writes downstream; a write-back model retaining ownership until one final eviction sends one final dirty-line write-back.

definition: A cache write policy in which a write updates only the cache's copy and marks it dirty; the new data is passed down to the next level later, for example when the line is evicted or another core requests it. It saves traffic when the same data is written repeatedly.
example: Assuming retained ownership and one final eviction, a million eight-byte stores to one line can produce one 64-byte write-back, versus 8 MB of unmerged forwarded stores in the write-through model.

definition: A small queue that holds stores on their way to the next memory level, so the processor does not have to wait for each one to complete. It can merge several stores to the same line, and a full buffer stalls further stores.

A queue that retains dirty victim data while write-back is pending, permitting other work, including a new fill, to overlap when resources allow. It does not guarantee that every write-back cost is hidden.
example: If buffering completely hides the stated 100-cycle write-back cost, a model with 40% dirty victims drops from 140 to 100 additional cycles per miss.

definition: A write-miss policy in which a store to a line not in the cache first allocates (and usually fetches) that line, then updates it in the cache. It suits data that will be read or written again soon and is the usual partner of write-back.

A write-miss policy in which a store that misses is sent straight to the next level without bringing the line into the cache. It suits data that will not be touched again and is the usual partner of write-through.

A coherence request that fetches a cache line and at the same time gains exclusive permission to write it, invalidating copies in other caches. A store that misses in a write-allocate cache usually issues one.

A lower cache level whose presence information covers every line in the specified upper levels. Evicting its entry requires invalidating those covered upper copies. Its data can be stale when an upper copy is dirty; inclusion can filter snoops but duplicates residency.
A cache arrangement in which a line lives in only one of the specified levels at a time, so their capacities add up without duplication. Lines typically move between levels on misses and evictions.

Neither inclusive nor exclusive: presence in one of the specified cache levels does not guarantee presence or absence in the other. Non-inclusive alone is weaker wording and does not necessarily exclude an exclusive organisation.

Cycles in which the processor cannot make progress because it is waiting for data from the memory hierarchy. In a blocking model they are the references per instruction times the miss rate times the miss penalty.

A cache that cannot accept another cache request while servicing a miss, or a simplified model treating requests serially. A processor can sometimes execute independent non-memory instructions meanwhile; assuming all miss time becomes core stall time is an additional modelling restriction.
Logic in the processor that spots access patterns, such as walking through an array, and fetches lines into the cache before the program asks for them, turning some misses into hits.

An implementation-specific store path, often requested with a non-temporal instruction, intended to reduce cache pollution or old-line fetching. Whether it allocates, combines full lines or avoids a read depends on the instruction, memory type, alignment and implementation.
example: In the stated ideal full-line model, a 64 MiB overwrite generates 64 MiB of writes instead of 64 MiB of fetches plus 64 MiB of later write-backs.

definition: A buffer that can merge stores to one memory region before issuing downstream writes. Full-line combining can reduce old-data reads in a suitable streaming-store path; partial buffers, memory types, instructions and ordering rules can require different transfers.
Combining several pending stores to the same cache line in a write buffer into a single transfer to the next level, reducing write-through traffic.

Removing a cache line, commonly to admit another line. Dirty data must be preserved when necessary, perhaps through a write-back buffer or coherence handover rather than a fully serial write-back before reuse.
The latency of the slowest small fraction of operations, such as the worst 1%. An average such as AMAT can look good while a few very slow accesses dominate the run time.

The storage element for one bit in DRAM: one transistor acting as a switch and one capacitor holding a small charge. Reading it disturbs the charge, and the charge leaks away, which is why DRAM needs sense amplifiers and refresh.
A DDR5 refresh mode that refreshes one chosen bank in each bank group at a time, so the other banks can keep serving requests, subject to timing rules.
A line of cells in a DRAM bank that is opened (activated) all at once into the row buffer; typically thousands of bits wide. Not the same thing as an operating-system page.

A DRAM read targeting the row already active in a bank. Once all other timing and command constraints are satisfied, the simplified READ-to-first-data interval is CAS latency; queueing and transfer completion add costs.
A DRAM read when no row is active in the target bank. In the simplified command path, activation-to-read delay plus CAS latency determines first data; other timing constraints may add delay.

A DRAM access to a different row from the one currently active in its bank. A simplified legal PRE, ACT, READ sequence pays precharge, activation-to-read and CAS delays; real queueing and earlier operations can add more.

DRAM devices operated together under a rank selection to supply the data width of an interface. A conventional 64-data-bit DDR4 rank can use eight eight-bit devices; DDR5 organises ranks within narrower sub-channel interfaces.

An independent array inside a DRAM chip with its own row buffer, so different banks can have different rows open and work in parallel. DDR4 and DDR5 also gather banks into bank groups with their own timing rules.
example: The illustrated DDR4 eight-bit device has 16 banks in four bank groups; other widths and generations can differ.

definition: Dual in-line memory module: the small circuit board of DRAM chips that plugs into a motherboard slot. A DIMM carries one or more ranks.
In DDR5, one of the two independent 32-bit halves of a DIMM's 64-bit data interface. Each has its own commands, so the controller can run two accesses at once on one module.

Transferring data on both the rising and the falling edge of a clock, so two transfers happen per clock cycle; it is what DDR stands for. The number in a name like DDR4-3200 is the transfer rate in MT/s, twice the clock frequency in MHz.
example: DDR4-3200 makes 3,200 million transfers per second on a 1,600 MHz clock.

definition: Mega-transfers per second: millions of data transfers on a bus each second. For DDR memory it is twice the clock frequency in MHz, because data moves twice per clock.
example: DDR5-4800 runs at 4,800 MT/s on a 2,400 MHz clock.

definition: Column address strobe latency: the number of memory clock cycles between a READ command to an open row and the first data appearing. It is quoted in cycles, so its time in nanoseconds depends on the clock speed.
example: DDR4-3200 CL22 means 22 cycles of 0.625 ns, which is 13.75 ns.

aliases: row address to column address delay
definition: Row-to-column delay: the minimum number of clock cycles between activating a DRAM row and reading a column from it.
Row precharge time: the minimum number of clock cycles needed to close the open row in a bank (precharge) before another row can be activated.
The DRAM activate command: it opens a row, copying it from the cells into the bank's row buffer so its columns can be read.
The DRAM precharge command: it closes the open row in a bank and resets the bit lines so another row can be activated.
The DRAM read command: it reads a burst of data from columns of the row currently open in a bank.

The number of data transfers in a DRAM burst. The illustrated DDR4 BL8 transfer on a 64-data-bit interface and DDR5 BL16 transfer on a 32-data-bit sub-channel each carry 64 bytes; supported burst modes vary.

First-ready, first-come-first-served: a memory scheduling family that prioritises ready commands or row hits and then age according to its specific rules. It can improve row locality but may introduce unfairness; real controller policies vary.
The maximum rate a memory channel can move data, equal to its data-transfer rate times its bus width. Real programs reach less because of refresh, row-buffer conflicts and too few requests in flight.
example: DDR4-3200 on a 64-bit channel: 3,200 million × 8 bytes = 25.6 GB/s.

definition: A queueing result: in a steady state, the average number of items in a system equals their arrival rate times the average time each spends inside. For memory, bandwidth equals bytes in flight divided by latency.
example: 64 lines of 64 bytes in flight with 80 ns latency sustain 51.2 GB/s.

definition: Issued memory requests whose responses are still outstanding. More independent requests can overlap latency, up to limits imposed by queues, dependencies, bandwidth, scheduling and contention.

Following loaded pointers to compute later addresses. One strictly dependent cold chain reveals its next demand address only after the previous load returns; other independent chains or capable prefetch engines can create additional concurrency.

Non-uniform memory access: the access cost depends on the relationship between a processor and the memory’s NUMA node. Nodes can be subdivisions of a socket and need not correspond one-to-one with sockets.

Memory on the NUMA node local to the executing CPU, contrasted with memory on another node. Remote accesses can traverse additional links within or between sockets; actual latency and bandwidth depend on topology and load.
Ultra Path Interconnect: Intel's point-to-point link between processor sockets, carrying remote memory accesses and coherence traffic.
AMD's interconnect between the dies and sockets of its processors, carrying memory and coherence traffic.

Under Linux local allocation policy, a fault allocating a fresh writable anonymous page normally prefers memory near the faulting CPU, subject to allowed nodes, capacity and fallback. Rewriting an already backed page does not by itself relocate it; migration and other policies can change placement.

A Linux tool for inspecting NUMA topology and launching programs with CPU and memory placement policies. numactl distance values express relative firmware topology costs rather than measured nanoseconds.
A NUMA policy that spreads a program's pages round-robin across nodes, balancing placement for large shared data at the cost of some remote accesses.
A Linux kernel feature that samples which nodes access each page and migrates pages towards the threads using them, at the cost of extra page faults.

An Intel hardware prefetcher that can use values loaded from memory to predict the addresses of later loads in some indirect-access patterns, unlike stream or stride prefetchers that only see addresses.
How many loop iterations ahead a software prefetch asks for data. It should be roughly the memory latency divided by the time per iteration, so the data arrives just before it is needed.
example: With 100 ns latency and 5 ns per iteration, a distance of about 20 iterations is a starting point.

definition: A GCC/Clang builtin that requests a prefetch hint for an address. GCC documents that the hint does not fault on an invalid target, but evaluating the address expression must still be valid; the compiler or processor may emit no useful prefetch.
Filling a cache with unhelpful data, such as unused prefetched lines, that can displace useful resident data and increase later misses.
Code whose speed is limited mainly by the memory system. Bandwidth limits cap data delivery; latency and dependent accesses can limit progress even before peak bandwidth is reached.

Code whose throughput is limited mainly by computation or other CPU execution resources rather than memory delivery. Reducing memory latency may have little effect until that dominant resource limit changes.
High-performance computing: running large scientific or engineering workloads on supercomputers and clusters, where memory bandwidth tuning matters a great deal.

Basic input/output system: a traditional name for PC platform firmware and its configuration interface, also used for some UEFI-based systems. Available controls, including prefetch settings, depend on the platform and firmware version.

A virtual-memory page without ordinary file backing, such as writable private heap or stack storage. Linux often allocates it lazily on a write fault; shared zero pages, eager population, reuse and explicit policy can change when physical storage is assigned.

In computer architecture, the rate at which data can be moved between parts of the system, such as between DRAM and the caches, usually given in bytes per second (GB/s). It is separate from latency: a memory system can deliver a lot of data per second while each individual access still takes tens of nanoseconds.
example: One DDR4-3200 channel has a peak bandwidth of 25.6 GB/s.

definition: Concurrent operations competing to modify shared data or obtain its lock. In a coherent system, repeated writers on different cores can cause ownership changes and retries; one retained owner can perform many writes without a transfer.
example: Eight threads incrementing one shared atomic counter all contend for the single cache line that holds it.

definition: Reading or writing successive positions in a defined order. A dense unit-stride numeric scan uses adjacent elements and may use every fetched byte; larger elements, record fields, alignment and partial scans can leave bytes unused.
example: Summing an array from index 0 upwards is a sequential scan.

definition: In computer hardware, one complete request-and-response exchange on a bus or interconnect, such as a cache asking for a line or telling other caches to invalidate theirs. Coherence protocols are described in terms of these transactions.
example: A BusRd is a bus transaction that asks for a copy of a line to read.

definition: In programming, a library type that holds a collection of elements, such as C++ std::vector, Java ArrayList or a Python list. Whether it stores the values themselves or references to them decides its memory layout and cache behaviour.
example: std::vector<double> stores raw doubles contiguously; ArrayList<Integer> stores references to boxed objects.

definition: The rules (line states and messages) by which hardware keeps cache coherence: private caches holding copies of one memory location agree on a single order of writes to it, so a write by one core is eventually seen by the others. In Architecture, 'coherence' on its own means this cache coherence; MESI is the textbook protocol.

The number of bytes in one cache line, the unit that a particular cache stores and transfers. This module uses explicit 64-byte and 128-byte models; actual geometry depends on the processor and cache level.
example: A 64-byte line holds eight eight-byte doubles or sixteen four-byte integers.

definition: A cache miss caused by the program's own load or store, as opposed to a request made by a prefetcher. Prefetching aims to turn demand misses into hits.

Error correction inside a DRAM chip; Micron’s described DDR5 implementation protects 128 data bits with eight check bits for single-error correction. It does not by itself protect the channel transfer, and does not replace memory-system ECC.

Prefetching requested by explicit hint instructions placed in the program (for example via __builtin_prefetch), rather than detected by hardware. The hint asks for a line early so a later load hits; the processor may ignore it.

A DRAM refresh operation affecting all banks in its addressed rank, which are unavailable for the specified recovery interval. Device timing and mode determine the duration; same-bank refresh instead targets a bank in each bank group.
example: In an illustrative model, 350 ns of blocking every 7,812.5 ns makes the addressed resources unavailable for 4.48% of the interval.

definition: The number of data bits one DRAM chip supplies per transfer, written ×4, ×8 or ×16. Chips are combined to fill a channel: eight ×8 chips make a 64-bit DDR4 rank.
An atomic read-modify-write operation that obtains an old flag value while setting it. A naive spinlock repeats this operation; test-and-test-and-set adds a read-polling stage before attempting it.

A C++ sequence container with bidirectional iteration and constant-time insertion or erasure at a known position. Its elements need not be contiguous; typical doubly linked implementations allocate nodes, unlike vector’s contiguous element storage.
A Linux tool for NUMA allocation statistics, with options for per-node system or process views. Its counters help investigate placement; they are not a measurement of individual DRAM-access latency.

A programming language with fixed-length arrays, dynamically sized slice views and built-in concurrency support. An array stores its element sequence in order; a slice of slices need not form one contiguous rectangular matrix.
